title: Load balancing
summary: Choose where new work goes using signals that match the work; equal call counts can hide very unequal demand.
overview: A load balancer selects a backend: one service instance able to handle a request. The routing unit matters. Transport-level balancing assigns connections; application-level balancing can assign individual requests or HTTP/2 streams. Round robin rotates through eligible instances without measuring their current workload. These distinctions are documented by gRPC and Envoy.
why: An agent that fans out repository searches can expose bottlenecks in a shared tool service. Investigate per-worker waiting time, outstanding calls, resource use, and failures before adding replicas or changing models. Those measurements help distinguish routing imbalance from exhausted capacity.
example: Imagine two identical repository-search workers, each with one execution slot. Short file lookups usually finish quickly; a full-tree scan takes longer. Round robin can send the next lookup behind that scan while the other worker is idle. The accompanying film is an illustrative schedule, not a benchmark or a production configuration.
judgment: Use request-aware routing when uneven request cost is an observed problem. Google SRE explains why outstanding-request counts can still misrepresent capacity, especially with unseen traffic or fast failures. Envoy’s equal-weight least-request policy samples candidates rather than necessarily scanning every host. Validate the deployed policy and version; neither algorithm promises optimal latency.
next: Where is routing decided in our tool path, what is counted there, and can we demonstrate waiting on one worker while another is idle?

learning.relevance: Use this chapter when concurrent agents share replicated tool services and traces reveal uneven waiting or utilization. A team learning delegation on one workstation should prioritize tool contracts, bounded concurrency, and evaluation before introducing balancing infrastructure.
outcomes: Identify whether a tool call is routed per connection or per request.
Use a trace to distinguish cumulative assignments, outstanding requests, and executing work.
Compare two routing policies under the same mixed-cost workload and explain a limitation.

workflow.before: An engineer launches searches sequentially and investigates slow jobs individually, with little simultaneous demand on the shared service.
workflow.after: An agent launches bounded concurrent searches through a measured routing layer; engineers replay representative traffic before changing its policy.
workflow.human: Own concurrency limits, service eligibility, permissions, rollback thresholds, and correctness checks. An instruction in an agent prompt does not enforce infrastructure limits or access control.

walkthrough: Map the real path from agent to tool client, proxy, and worker. Check whether multiple calls share a connection. gRPC documents how an application-aware proxy can distribute HTTP/2 streams; adding workers does not itself move an existing connection.

Replay a small workload with fixed arrivals: several short lookups and one long scan. Record assignment, execution start, completion, and backend. A request waiting at a worker remains outstanding to the caller even though it is not executing.

Compare round robin with a toy least-outstanding dispatcher. In the film, A has a running scan and queued Q4; B is idle. New Q5 and then Q6 go to B after the policy changes, visibly breaking rotation. Q4 stays on A until the scan finishes. Routing new work does not migrate existing work.

Compare waiting and completion times, errors, and resource saturation. If all workers fill, change admission limits or capacity. Envoy documents separate limits for pending requests, outstanding requests, and retries; balancing alone supplies none of that extra capacity.

Rehearse removing a worker before rollout. Envoy documents explicit drain controls and protocol-specific behavior, so test your shutdown sequence instead of assuming a successful health response or a termination signal guarantees a clean drain.
pitfalls: Counting requests instead of measuring cost: equal assignments can conceal a long-running task.
Treating fewer outstanding calls as guaranteed spare capacity; fast errors or other clients can make that signal misleading.
Replaying state-changing tool calls to fix distribution; the demo uses read-only work and establishes no retry safety.

exercise.title: Find the idle worker
steps: Create two local single-slot worker stubs with FIFO queues; use read-only simulated tasks.
Send six fixed arrivals, mixing 200 ms tasks with one 2 s task; log arrival, assignment, start, and finish.
Replay exactly that schedule with round robin and least outstanding, counting both running and queued calls.
Compare individual waits and maximum queue depth; repeat with both workers occupied and record why routing alone cannot remove all waiting.
success: Show an actual trace where work waits while another worker is idle, or explain why your chosen arrivals never create that condition.
Explain one measured difference without claiming universal improvement; confirm every request completes once and existing work is never moved.
